title: Head in the Clouds
full_review:
In "Head in the Clouds" (Sony Classics), writer-director John Duigan tries hard to emulate those old-fashioned romantic sagas of lovers who come together and part over the years, but the resulting film, while handsomely designed and photographed, proves only fitfully engaging.

The action begins in the 1930s at Cambridge University when free spirit Gilda (Charlize Theron) takes shelter from the rain in the room of student Guy (Stuart Townsend), a decent Irishman on scholarship. She's having an affair with a don there, so the night she spends with Guy is chaste, though there's an immediate attraction.

Before long, they consummate their relationship, thus initiating a romance that picks up after Gilda moves to Paris and begins to make her mark as a photographer. She lives with Mia (Penelope Cruz), a Spanish model and sometime stripper, and has various lovers. Before long, Guy moves in as Gilda's lover, and the trio forms a cozy threesome that presumably stops just short of the sexual, though they seem to enjoy same-bed snuggling.

Gilda cares only for her happiness, her comfortable setup with Guy and Mia, and her own career advancement, but both Guy and Mia have more of a social conscience, so eventually Guy decides to go to Spain to support the Republican army and fight fascism, while Mia -- after being roughed up by a kinky gallery owner -- opts to return there as well and become a nurse. (Unbeknownst to the others, Gilda makes an assignation with the cad who hurt Mia -- and gives him back some of his own -- in an S&M scene.) Gilda feels totally betrayed by what she views as their abandonment. She tells them both they should stop feeling guilty about the world's troubles.

Inevitably, Guy and Mia's paths cross in Spain and, of course, they make love. "She'd be pleased," declares Mia of Gilda, emblematic of these characters' amoral outlook.

Later, Guy becomes a spy for British intelligence and works with the underground in Nazi-occupied Paris, while Gilda, who has severed contact with him, takes on a Nazi lover (Thomas Kretschmann). Once the film moves into this phase, the waning pace picks up as the espionage elements of the plot come to the fore.

In the follow-up role to her Oscar-winning "Monster," Theron doesn't quite generate the old-style glamour the role calls for here. She looks smashing in her period outfits, but her flatly accented American line readings are strictly 2004. Townsend is a sympathetic lead, as the story is really seen through his eyes. There's a touch of blandness in his performance, but that could be the passivity of the character. And Cruz -- who spends much of the movie looking glumly tousled or bruised -- is adequate in the second-banana role.

The menage a trois they form is meant to be endearing in a bohemian sort of way -- and is it by chance that Theron's hedonistic character is named Gilda, like the character in Noel Coward's scintillating menage-a-trois comedy, "Design for Living"? -- but there's little real chemistry to make that plausible.

A couple of the encounters between Guy and Gilda are intensely passionate and graphic, though there's minimal nudity, except for a languorous bathtub scene where Gilda bares her breasts.

The film is beautifully designed, and all the period trappings are eye-filling, but -- as a sweeping love story against a tumultuous wartime backdrop -- "Head in the Clouds" is a far cry from "A Farewell to Arms," "The English Patient" or "Dr. Zhivago" in its depiction of lovers thwarted by the onrush of world events.

Because of an overall freewheeling attitude toward sex, a fleeting orgy tableau, intense sexual encounters, some rough and crude language, nudity, sadomasochism, torture, a gory shooting and a crude episode of urination, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
